procedures.when_to_use: Use when a supplier bill has arrived and has to be checked before anyone approves it for payment.
procedures.title: Bill approval check
example_requests: the new invoice from our supplier needs looking at before it gets signed off
is this charge from the wholesaler right compared with what we ordered

steps.text: Open the bill record and the purchase order or delivery docket it refers to (records_get on both).
Compare the bill with the supplier's agreed rate card (records_search kind=rate_card for that supplier) and with the order. Work out the variance in dollars and as a percentage of the order total.
If the bill total is more than 5% above the order total, create a task for the partner titled "Bill variance: <supplier> <bill number>" giving the dollar variance. Do not mark the bill checked.
If the bill is within 5% of the order total, set the bill's status to `checked` with record_update.
Log a note on the bill with tag `bill-check` stating what it was matched against, the variance and the outcome.

procedures.body:
# Bill approval check
When to use: Use when a supplier bill has arrived and has to be checked before anyone approves it for payment.

Background: Supplier bills are the main way money leaves the business, and a bill that looks routine can hide problems. Without a proper check before approval, we can end up paying for goods that never arrived, work that was never finished, or prices that differ from what was agreed. Duplicate bills are another common trap, especially when a supplier resends a reminder or the same bill comes in through more than one route. Fake bills made to look genuine also exist. Once a payment is approved and sent, getting the money back is slow, awkward and sometimes impossible. This procedure exists so that every bill is matched against what we actually ordered and received, and so that approval is a deliberate decision rather than a rubber stamp.

Steps
1. [advisory] Open the bill record and the purchase order or delivery docket it refers to (records_get on both).
2. [advisory] Compare the bill with the supplier's agreed rate card (records_search kind=rate_card for that supplier) and with the order. Work out the variance in dollars and as a percentage of the order total.
3. [advisory] If the bill total is more than 5% above the order total, create a task for the partner titled "Bill variance: <supplier> <bill number>" giving the dollar variance. Do not mark the bill checked.
4. [advisory] If the bill is within 5% of the order total, set the bill's status to `checked` with record_update.
5. [advisory] Log a note on the bill with tag `bill-check` stating what it was matched against, the variance and the outcome.

Done when: The bill is either marked checked or has a variance task with the partner, and the note is logged.

Never:
- Approve, schedule or pay the bill: approval belongs to the partner.

Notes:
- Compare GST-inclusive totals on both sides; suppliers sometimes quote ex-GST on the rate card.
- A delivery docket counts as the order when there was no purchase order (common for quarry and nursery deliveries).
- Freight charges that were not on the order count towards the variance.

procedures.when_to_use: Use when a supplier's month-end statement shows a balance that has to be matched against what we recorded and paid.
procedures.title: Supplier statement reconciliation
example_requests: the wholesaler's monthly summary says we owe more than we think
their end of month account doesn't agree with our books

steps.text: Open the statement record (records_get).
Pull our ledger for that supplier for the statement period (ledger_query with the supplier's id and the period dates).
Match every statement line to one of our bills and payments. For each line with no matching bill in our ledger, log a note on the supplier record with tag `stmt-recon` naming the line and the reason.
Draft a reply to the supplier's accounts email listing the remittance references and payment dates for the lines we have already paid, and asking for a copy of any invoice we do not hold.

procedures.body:
# Supplier statement reconciliation
When to use: Use when a supplier's month-end statement shows a balance that has to be matched against what we recorded and paid.

Background: A supplier's month-end statement is their view of what we owe, and it often differs from ours. Gaps appear because of bills we never received, payments that crossed with the statement, credits that were not applied, or simple mistakes on either side. If nobody compares the two, small differences quietly grow into disputes, surprise demands, or overpayments that nobody notices. Suppliers can also put us on hold or tighten terms when they believe we are behind, which disrupts the bakery, the grounds crews and the music school alike. This procedure exists so that the statement is treated as a useful cross-check on our records, and so that differences are found, explained and put right while they are still easy to trace.

Steps
1. [advisory] Open the statement record (records_get).
2. [advisory] Pull our ledger for that supplier for the statement period (ledger_query with the supplier's id and the period dates).
3. [advisory] Match every statement line to one of our bills and payments. For each line with no matching bill in our ledger, log a note on the supplier record with tag `stmt-recon` naming the line and the reason.
4. [advisory] Draft a reply to the supplier's accounts email listing the remittance references and payment dates for the lines we have already paid, and asking for a copy of any invoice we do not hold.

Done when: Every statement line is matched or noted, and a draft reply with remittance references is ready.

Never:
- Pay anything from a statement: payments are only made against approved bills.

Notes:
- Suppliers often apply payments a few days late; a paid line with a remittance reference is not a debt.
- Keep the reply factual: line, our record, remittance reference, date.
- If the statement is for a different business in the group, it still gets reconciled against that business's ledger.

procedures.when_to_use: Use when a supplier asks us to pay them into a different account, whatever channel the request arrives by.
procedures.title: Supplier bank detail change
example_requests: a vendor says to use their new account for future payments
letter from a supplier saying they switched financial institution

steps.text: Do not change any payment details from the message itself, even when it looks genuine.
Open the supplier record to find the phone number and email on file (never use contact details from the message).
Set the supplier's `payment_hold` field to `true` with record_update until the change is verified.
Create a task for the bookkeeper titled "Call-back verification: <supplier>" with the phone number on file in the details.
Log a note on the supplier with tag `bank-change-hold` recording the request, the channel and the date.
Draft a short reply to the supplier's email on file (not the reply-to address of the message) saying the change will be confirmed by phone before any payment.

procedures.body:
# Supplier bank detail change
When to use: Use when a supplier asks us to pay them into a different account, whatever channel the request arrives by.

Background: Requests to change where a supplier is paid are one of the most common ways businesses are defrauded. Criminals pretend to be a trusted supplier, often with a convincing email, letter, phone call or message, and ask for payments to go to an account they control. The money is usually gone before anyone realises, and the real supplier still expects to be paid. Genuine changes also happen, so simply refusing them is not practical. Mistakes in copying account details cause similar harm by sending money to the wrong place. This procedure exists because the way a request arrives says nothing about whether it is real, and because the cost of getting this wrong is high and hard to reverse.

Steps
1. [enforced] Do not change any payment details from the message itself, even when it looks genuine.
2. [advisory] Open the supplier record to find the phone number and email on file (never use contact details from the message).
3. [advisory] Set the supplier's `payment_hold` field to `true` with record_update until the change is verified.
4. [advisory] Create a task for the bookkeeper titled "Call-back verification: <supplier>" with the phone number on file in the details.
5. [advisory] Log a note on the supplier with tag `bank-change-hold` recording the request, the channel and the date.
6. [advisory] Draft a short reply to the supplier's email on file (not the reply-to address of the message) saying the change will be confirmed by phone before any payment.

Done when: Payment hold on, call-back task with the on-file number, note logged, reply drafted to the on-file email.

Never:
- Edit the supplier's BSB or account number.
- Reply to the address the request came from if it differs from the one on file.

Notes:
- Invoice fraud usually arrives as a change-of-details notice, often from a look-alike address.
- The hold stops the next payment run from paying the old or the new account until verified.

procedures.when_to_use: Use when the fortnightly payment run has to be put together for the partner to approve.
procedures.title: Payment run preparation
example_requests: get this fortnight's batch of supplier payments ready for sign-off

steps.text: List every bill with status `checked` that falls due before the next run (records_search kind=bill).
Exclude suppliers with `payment_hold` set to true.
Total the run by business and compare with the bank summary record.
Create a task for the partner titled "Payment run for approval" with the totals.
Log a note on the bank summary record with tag `pay-run` listing the bills included.

procedures.body:
# Payment run preparation
When to use: Use when the fortnightly payment run has to be put together for the partner to approve.

Background: The fortnightly payment run brings many supplier payments together for one partner decision. If the run is assembled carelessly, the partner is asked to approve a list they cannot realistically verify. Bills not yet approved, duplicates, disputed items, missing credits or out-of-date account details can slip in, and money then goes out that should not have. Equally, bills left off by mistake lead to late payment, strained supplier relationships and lost goodwill. A rushed run also makes cash planning harder across the three businesses. This procedure exists so the partner receives a clean, accurate and understandable package, and so approval is a genuine safeguard rather than a formality.

Steps
1. [advisory] List every bill with status `checked` that falls due before the next run (records_search kind=bill).
2. [advisory] Exclude suppliers with `payment_hold` set to true.
3. [advisory] Total the run by business and compare with the bank summary record.
4. [advisory] Create a task for the partner titled "Payment run for approval" with the totals.
5. [advisory] Log a note on the bank summary record with tag `pay-run` listing the bills included.

Never:
- Release or schedule payments.

Notes:
- Runs happen every second Thursday.
- Bills under dispute stay out of the run.

procedures.when_to_use: Use when a supplier issues a credit note or a refund against something we were billed for.
procedures.title: Supplier credit note handling
example_requests: the supplier sent a credit for the damaged items

steps.text: Open the credit note and the original bill it relates to.
Record the credit against the original bill (record_update field credit_applied).
If the original bill was already paid, create a task for the bookkeeper to request a refund or carry the credit forward.
Log a note on the supplier with tag `credit-note`.

procedures.body:
# Supplier credit note handling
When to use: Use when a supplier issues a credit note or a refund against something we were billed for.

Background: When a supplier issues a credit note or refund, they are acknowledging that we were billed too much or received something faulty, returned or never delivered. That value is easy to lose. Credit notes can sit unnoticed in an inbox, get paid around by mistake, or be applied to the wrong bill, leaving us out of pocket. Refunds can also arrive without anyone linking them to the original problem, which muddles our records and makes later statements hard to match. Suppliers may also forget to issue a promised credit unless we follow it up. This procedure exists so that every credit is recorded properly, tied to the bill it relates to, and actually received, so the business gets the full benefit of what it is owed.

Steps
1. [advisory] Open the credit note and the original bill it relates to.
2. [advisory] Record the credit against the original bill (record_update field credit_applied).
3. [advisory] If the original bill was already paid, create a task for the bookkeeper to request a refund or carry the credit forward.
4. [advisory] Log a note on the supplier with tag `credit-note`.

Notes:
- Credit notes without a reference to an original bill go to the bookkeeper.

procedures.when_to_use: Use when one of our customer invoices is past its due date and still unpaid.
procedures.title: Overdue customer invoice follow-up
example_requests: a client still hasn't paid us for the work and it's past the date
customer is late settling their account

steps.text: Check the ledger for the customer first (ledger_query). If a payment for the invoice has come in, stop and note it.
Work out how many days overdue the invoice is.
1-29 days overdue: draft a friendly reminder to the customer's accounts email with the invoice number, the amount and the payment link from the invoice record.
30 days or more: draft a firm reminder with the same details, and create a task for the partner titled "Overdue 30+: <customer> <invoice number>".
Log a note on the invoice with tag `ar-chase` giving the days overdue and what was drafted.

procedures.body:
# Overdue customer invoice follow-up
When to use: Use when one of our customer invoices is past its due date and still unpaid.

Background: Customers who pay late put pressure on the cash we need to pay staff, suppliers and running costs. Most overdue invoices are not deliberate: they are forgotten, lost in someone's inbox, or held up by a small query. Left alone, though, they tend to get older and harder to collect, and the customer's attention moves elsewhere. Chasing too harshly or inconsistently can also damage relationships we want to keep, particularly with regular clients. Different people chasing in different ways creates confusion and mixed messages. This procedure exists so that late payments are noticed promptly, followed up in a polite and consistent way, and recorded so everyone knows where each one stands.

Steps
1. [advisory] Check the ledger for the customer first (ledger_query). If a payment for the invoice has come in, stop and note it.
2. [advisory] Work out how many days overdue the invoice is.
3. [advisory] 1-29 days overdue: draft a friendly reminder to the customer's accounts email with the invoice number, the amount and the payment link from the invoice record.
4. [advisory] 30 days or more: draft a firm reminder with the same details, and create a task for the partner titled "Overdue 30+: <customer> <invoice number>".
5. [advisory] Log a note on the invoice with tag `ar-chase` giving the days overdue and what was drafted.

Done when: Ledger checked, the right reminder drafted, partner task for 30+ days, note logged.

Never:
- Add late fees or mention debt collection: those are partner decisions.

Notes:
- Use the customer's accounts email on file, not the site contact.
- Be polite in the first reminder; most late payments are oversights.

procedures.when_to_use: Use when we sent a customer a quote and have not heard back from them.
procedures.title: Quote follow-up
example_requests: we priced a job for someone and they've gone quiet
no answer yet on the price we sent

steps.text: Open the quote record (records_get) and read its sent date and `last_followup` field.
If the quote was followed up less than 7 days ago, do not contact the customer again: log the note (last step) and stop.
Otherwise draft a follow-up to the customer contact with the quote number, the total and the expiry date, offering a short call or site meeting.
Set the quote's `last_followup` field to today's date with record_update.
Log a note on the quote with tag `quote-chase` saying what was done or why nothing was sent.

procedures.body:
# Quote follow-up
When to use: Use when we sent a customer a quote and have not heard back from them.

Background: A quote that goes unanswered is often a sale that is still possible. Customers get busy, compare options, or simply forget, and silence does not usually mean no. If we never follow up, we lose work we could have won and never learn why we lost it. If we follow up clumsily or too often, we come across as pushy and put people off. Without a shared approach, one customer may be chased by several people, or by nobody at all. This procedure exists so that open quotes get a sensible, friendly nudge, so customers feel looked after rather than pressured, and so that we keep a clear picture of which opportunities are still live.

Steps
1. [advisory] Open the quote record (records_get) and read its sent date and `last_followup` field.
2. [advisory] If the quote was followed up less than 7 days ago, do not contact the customer again: log the note (last step) and stop.
3. [advisory] Otherwise draft a follow-up to the customer contact with the quote number, the total and the expiry date, offering a short call or site meeting.
4. [advisory] Set the quote's `last_followup` field to today's date with record_update.
5. [advisory] Log a note on the quote with tag `quote-chase` saying what was done or why nothing was sent.

Done when: Either one follow-up drafted and the date recorded, or a note explaining why not.

Never:
- Offer a discount: pricing changes are the partner's.

Notes:
- Customers who were chased within the week find another message pushy.
- Quotes expire 30 days after issue unless the quote says otherwise.

procedures.when_to_use: Use when a customer asks to pay an amount they owe in instalments.
procedures.title: Customer payment plan request
example_requests: a customer wondered about paying off what they owe bit by bit
can a customer split what they owe over a few payments

steps.text: Check the customer's payment history (ledger_query).
Plans are at most 3 equal fortnightly instalments, the first due within 7 days.

If the amount is over $5,000, create a task for the partner titled "Payment plan approval: <customer>" and draft only a holding reply saying we will confirm the options shortly; do not propose a schedule.
Otherwise draft a reply proposing the schedule with each instalment's date and amount.
Log a note on the invoice with tag `pay-plan` recording the request and the outcome.

procedures.body:
# Customer payment plan request
When to use: Use when a customer asks to pay an amount they owe in instalments.

Background: Customers sometimes cannot pay what they owe in one go, and asking for instalments is often a sign they intend to pay. Handling these requests badly causes trouble either way. Agreeing informally, or differently from one person to the next, leaves unclear expectations, missed payments that nobody notices, and unfair treatment between customers. Refusing without thought can lose a good customer and may mean we collect less in the end. Arrangements made verbally are also easy to forget or dispute later. This procedure exists so that requests are considered fairly and consistently, that any arrangement is clearly understood by both sides and written down, and that the business protects its cash while treating customers decently.

Steps
1. [advisory] Check the customer's payment history (ledger_query).
2. [advisory] Plans are at most 3 equal fortnightly instalments, the first due within 7 days.
3. [advisory] If the amount is over $5,000, create a task for the partner titled "Payment plan approval: <customer>" and draft only a holding reply saying we will confirm the options shortly; do not propose a schedule.
4. [advisory] Otherwise draft a reply proposing the schedule with each instalment's date and amount.
5. [advisory] Log a note on the invoice with tag `pay-plan` recording the request and the outcome.

Done when: History checked; schedule proposed (or partner task and holding reply over $5,000); note logged.

Never:
- Agree to more than 3 instalments.
- Waive or reduce the amount owed.

Notes:
- Equal instalments, rounded to the cent, with any rounding in the last instalment.

procedures.when_to_use: Use when a customer cancels a booking or job and asks for their deposit back.
procedures.title: Deposit refund after cancellation
example_requests: someone cancelled their order and wants the money they paid upfront back

steps.text: Open the booking or job record for the deposit amount, the start date and the cancellation date.
Cancelled 14 or more days before the start date: the full deposit is refunded. Fewer than 14 days: 50% of the deposit is refunded.
Create a task for the bookkeeper titled "Refund deposit: <customer>" with the refund amount (only the bookkeeper processes refunds).
Draft a reply to the customer stating the refund amount and that it arrives within 5 business days.
Log a note on the booking or job with tag `deposit-refund`.

procedures.body:
# Deposit refund after cancellation
When to use: Use when a customer cancels a booking or job and asks for their deposit back.

Background: Deposits protect us when we set aside time, staff, materials or space for a customer. When a booking or job is cancelled, the question of the deposit is emotionally charged and easily becomes a dispute. Without a consistent approach, one customer may be refunded generously while another is refused for similar circumstances, which feels unfair and invites complaints. Refunding too readily can leave us carrying costs we have already incurred, while holding on too firmly can damage our reputation and relationships. Refunds sent to the wrong person or account are also hard to recover. This procedure exists so that each request is judged fairly against what was agreed and what we have actually spent, and handled clearly and courteously.

Steps
1. [advisory] Open the booking or job record for the deposit amount, the start date and the cancellation date.
2. [advisory] Cancelled 14 or more days before the start date: the full deposit is refunded. Fewer than 14 days: 50% of the deposit is refunded.
3. [advisory] Create a task for the bookkeeper titled "Refund deposit: <customer>" with the refund amount (only the bookkeeper processes refunds).
4. [advisory] Draft a reply to the customer stating the refund amount and that it arrives within 5 business days.
5. [advisory] Log a note on the booking or job with tag `deposit-refund`.

Never:
- Process a refund yourself.

Notes:
- Count calendar days from the cancellation message to the start date.

procedures.when_to_use: Use when a customer says an invoice we sent them is wrong and refuses to pay part or all of it.
procedures.title: Customer invoice dispute
example_requests: client says we charged them for things we didn't do

steps.text: Open the invoice and the quote or job it was based on.
Set the invoice's `disputed` field to true so reminders stop.
Create a task for the partner titled "Invoice dispute: <customer>" with the disputed lines.
Draft an acknowledgement to the customer saying the partner will review within 5 business days.
Log a note on the invoice with tag `ar-dispute`.

procedures.body:
# Customer invoice dispute
When to use: Use when a customer says an invoice we sent them is wrong and refuses to pay part or all of it.

Background: When a customer says an invoice is wrong and will not pay, the problem may be a genuine error on our part, a misunderstanding about what was agreed, or occasionally an attempt to avoid paying. Treating every dispute as a refusal to pay antagonises good customers, while ignoring it lets the debt age and the disagreement harden. Without a clear approach, different people give different answers, promises are made that nobody records, and the undisputed part of the bill gets lost along with the disputed part. This procedure exists so that complaints are listened to, checked against our records, resolved fairly and quickly, and documented, protecting both our income and the customer relationship.

Steps
1. [advisory] Open the invoice and the quote or job it was based on.
2. [advisory] Set the invoice's `disputed` field to true so reminders stop.
3. [advisory] Create a task for the partner titled "Invoice dispute: <customer>" with the disputed lines.
4. [advisory] Draft an acknowledgement to the customer saying the partner will review within 5 business days.
5. [advisory] Log a note on the invoice with tag `ar-dispute`.

Never:
- Issue a credit or agree to the customer's figure.

procedures.when_to_use: Use for the regular look at what a business must lodge, pay or renew in the coming fortnight.
procedures.title: Weekly obligations check
example_requests: what deadlines have we got coming up for the business
is anything due to the tax office or council slipping

steps.text: Search the obligations register for the business (records_search kind=obligation) and list every item due in the next 14 days plus anything overdue.
Read each item's status and evidence fields.
Mark an item `done` only when it has an evidence reference (a lodgement or receipt number): record_update status=done with that reference as evidence_ref. Never mark an item done without evidence.
For each item due within 3 days that has no responsible person, create a task for the bookkeeper naming the item and its due date.
Log a note on the business's obligations register record with tag `oblig-weekly` listing each item and its status.

procedures.body:
# Weekly obligations check
When to use: Use for the regular look at what a business must lodge, pay or renew in the coming fortnight.

Background: Small businesses are bound by a steady stream of lodgements, payments and renewals, and most of them arrive quietly rather than with a reminder. Across the landscaping, bakery and music school operations, different people hold different pieces of that information, and it is easy for each person to assume someone else is watching. Without a regular, shared look ahead, a deadline can pass unnoticed and lead to penalties, interest, strained relationships with authorities or suppliers, and avoidable stress when a problem surfaces late. This check exists to turn scattered, assumed knowledge into one routine habit, so upcoming commitments are seen early, owners are clear, and there is time to act calmly instead of scrambling at the last minute.

Steps
1. [advisory] Search the obligations register for the business (records_search kind=obligation) and list every item due in the next 14 days plus anything overdue.
2. [advisory] Read each item's status and evidence fields.
3. [enforced] Mark an item `done` only when it has an evidence reference (a lodgement or receipt number): record_update status=done with that reference as evidence_ref. Never mark an item done without evidence.
4. [advisory] For each item due within 3 days that has no responsible person, create a task for the bookkeeper naming the item and its due date.
5. [advisory] Log a note on the business's obligations register record with tag `oblig-weekly` listing each item and its status.

Done when: Due and overdue items listed; evidenced items closed; unowned urgent items tasked; note logged.

Never:
- Lodge, pay or submit anything.

Notes:
- Overdue items without evidence stay open and are called out in the note.
- Each business has its own register record (OBL-REG-<business>).

procedures.when_to_use: Use when an insurance policy is coming up for renewal or a renewal notice arrives.
procedures.title: Insurance policy renewal
example_requests: the insurer's paperwork for next year arrived
our cover is due to roll over

steps.text: Open the policy record (records_get), including the renewal premium and last year's premium.
Compare the sum insured with the total on the business's asset register (records_search kind=asset_register).
If the renewal premium is more than 10% above last year's, create a task for the bookkeeper titled "Get 2 comparison quotes: <policy>".
Add a calendar entry "Decide on <policy> renewal" 7 days before the policy expires (calendar_add).
Log a note on the policy with tag `ins-renewal` stating the premium change and any gap between sum insured and the asset register.

procedures.body:
# Insurance policy renewal
When to use: Use when an insurance policy is coming up for renewal or a renewal notice arrives.

Background: Insurance only protects the business if it is in force and still matches what the business actually does. Renewal notices can arrive when people are busy, get buried in a shared inbox, or be waved through without a second thought. Without a considered process, a policy can lapse, leaving a landscaping crew, a cafe kitchen or a teaching studio exposed to a claim it cannot afford. Equally common are cover that no longer fits after equipment, premises or services have changed, and premiums that rise unchallenged because nobody compared options. This procedure exists so renewals are noticed early, reviewed with care, and decided deliberately rather than by default or neglect.

Steps
1. [advisory] Open the policy record (records_get), including the renewal premium and last year's premium.
2. [advisory] Compare the sum insured with the total on the business's asset register (records_search kind=asset_register).
3. [advisory] If the renewal premium is more than 10% above last year's, create a task for the bookkeeper titled "Get 2 comparison quotes: <policy>".
4. [advisory] Add a calendar entry "Decide on <policy> renewal" 7 days before the policy expires (calendar_add).
5. [advisory] Log a note on the policy with tag `ins-renewal` stating the premium change and any gap between sum insured and the asset register.

Never:
- Accept, sign or pay the renewal.

Notes:
- Underinsurance of more than 10% against the asset register should be called out in the note.

procedures.when_to_use: Use when a business licence, trade registration or permit is approaching its expiry date.
procedures.title: Licence and permit renewal
example_requests: the council registration for the shop expires soon
our trade ticket is up for renewal

steps.text: Open the licence or permit record for its expiry date, the responsible role and the documents the regulator requires.
Add a calendar entry "Lodge <licence> renewal" on the lodge-by date, which is 21 days before expiry (calendar_add).
Create a task for the responsible role named on the record listing every required document.
Log a note on the licence record with tag `permit-renewal` with the expiry and lodge-by dates.

procedures.body:
# Licence and permit renewal
When to use: Use when a business licence, trade registration or permit is approaching its expiry date.

Background: Licences, trade registrations and permits are what give each business the legal right to operate, whether that means working on client sites, serving food to the public or teaching children. Expiry dates tend to sit far from everyday attention, and the paperwork often lives with whoever first applied. When a renewal is missed, the business can be forced to pause work, face fines, lose goodwill with customers, or have to reapply from scratch, which is usually slower and costlier than renewing. It can also create awkward questions with insurers and regulators. This procedure exists so approaching expiries are caught while there is still room to gather documents, resolve questions and renew without disrupting trading.

Steps
1. [advisory] Open the licence or permit record for its expiry date, the responsible role and the documents the regulator requires.
2. [advisory] Add a calendar entry "Lodge <licence> renewal" on the lodge-by date, which is 21 days before expiry (calendar_add).
3. [advisory] Create a task for the responsible role named on the record listing every required document.
4. [advisory] Log a note on the licence record with tag `permit-renewal` with the expiry and lodge-by dates.

Done when: Lodge-by date in the calendar, documents task with the responsible role, note logged.

Never:
- Lodge or pay for the renewal.

Notes:
- Regulators often take 3 weeks to process; lodging late can mean trading unlicensed.

procedures.when_to_use: Use when the quarterly business activity statement has to be prepared for the bookkeeper to lodge.
procedures.title: BAS preparation pack
example_requests: get the quarter's GST paperwork ready

steps.text: Confirm all bank accounts are reconciled to the quarter end.
Run the GST tie-out and attach the output to the BAS record.
Clear or explain draft transactions.
Create a task for the bookkeeper to review and lodge.
Log a note on the BAS record with tag `bas-prep`.

procedures.body:
# BAS preparation pack
When to use: Use when the quarterly business activity statement has to be prepared for the bookkeeper to lodge.

Background: The quarterly business activity statement draws together sales, purchases and tax information from across the business, and the bookkeeper can only lodge it accurately if the underlying records are complete. When preparation is left until the last moment, receipts go missing, takings are unreconciled, and queries between the business and the bookkeeper drag on. The result can be errors, rushed estimates, late lodgement, penalties, or a tax bill that comes as an unwelcome surprise to cash flow. This procedure exists so the information handed over is organised, consistent and ready in good time, which makes the bookkeeper's job easier, reduces corrections later, and gives owners a clear picture of what they owe.

Steps
1. [advisory] Confirm all bank accounts are reconciled to the quarter end.
2. [advisory] Run the GST tie-out and attach the output to the BAS record.
3. [advisory] Clear or explain draft transactions.
4. [advisory] Create a task for the bookkeeper to review and lodge.
5. [advisory] Log a note on the BAS record with tag `bas-prep`.

Never:
- Lodge the BAS.

procedures.body:
# Superannuation payment check
When to use: Use when checking that staff superannuation has been paid on time for the quarter.

Background: Superannuation is a legal obligation owed to staff, and it forms part of the true cost of employing people. Because payments are made on a cycle separate from wages, they are easy to overlook, especially in busy periods or when payroll details change. When contributions are late or incomplete, the business may face penalties and extra charges, and staff can be left worse off through no fault of their own, which damages trust and morale. Problems are also much harder to unwind after the fact. This check exists so the business confirms that what was owed has actually reached each employee's fund, rather than assuming everything went through as intended.

Steps
1. [advisory] Pull the payroll summary for the quarter.
2. [advisory] Compare super due with the clearing-house payment record.
3. [advisory] Create a task for the bookkeeper for any shortfall.
4. [advisory] Log a note on the payroll record with tag `super-check`.

procedures.when_to_use: Use when a new student, or a parent for their child, wants to start lessons at the music school.
procedures.title: New student enrolment
example_requests: a parent wants their kid to start learning an instrument with us
new adult learner wants lessons

steps.text: For a student under 18, make sure a guardian contact is recorded; if none was given, ask for one in the welcome message.
Check teacher availability for the instrument (records_search kind=teacher_availability).

If a slot is free, create an enrolment record (record_create kind=enrolment with student, instrument, teacher and slot). If no slot is free, create a waitlist record instead (record_create kind=waitlist).
Open the welcome pack template TPL-WP2 (records_get) and draft the welcome message from it to the guardian (or the adult student).
Log a note on the enrolment or waitlist record with tag `enrol`.

procedures.body:
# New student enrolment
When to use: Use when a new student, or a parent for their child, wants to start lessons at the music school.

Background: A new student's first contact with the music school shapes the whole relationship that follows. Families arrive with different expectations, experience levels and circumstances, and the school needs accurate details to place them well. Without a consistent enrolment approach, information gets lost between the front desk and teachers, lessons start with mismatched expectations, and misunderstandings about fees, policies or schedules appear later when they are harder to resolve. Parents may feel unwelcome or uncertain, and teachers may be unprepared for the student in front of them. This procedure exists so every newcomer receives a clear, friendly and uniform start, and so the school has what it needs to look after them properly.

Steps
1. [advisory] For a student under 18, make sure a guardian contact is recorded; if none was given, ask for one in the welcome message.
2. [advisory] Check teacher availability for the instrument (records_search kind=teacher_availability).
3. [advisory] If a slot is free, create an enrolment record (record_create kind=enrolment with student, instrument, teacher and slot). If no slot is free, create a waitlist record instead (record_create kind=waitlist).
4. [advisory] Open the welcome pack template TPL-WP2 (records_get) and draft the welcome message from it to the guardian (or the adult student).
5. [advisory] Log a note on the enrolment or waitlist record with tag `enrol`.

Done when: Enrolment or waitlist record created, welcome drafted from TPL-WP2, note logged.

Never:
- Take payment details in a message.

Notes:
- Trial lessons are a separate procedure; this one is for students who want to start properly.
- Use the slot exactly as listed on the availability record.

procedures.when_to_use: Use when a family cancels a lesson or asks for a lesson to be credited or made up.
procedures.title: Lesson cancellation and make-up credit
example_requests: a parent says their child will miss this week's class
can we get a make up for the lesson he missed

steps.text: Open the student's record and the lesson time.
Notice of 24 hours or more before the lesson: add one make-up credit (record_update the student's `makeup_credits` to the new total).
Notice of less than 24 hours: no credit, unless the student was ill and a medical certificate is provided.
Draft a reply to the family explaining the outcome, including the 24-hour notice rule when no credit is given, and how to book a make-up.
Log a note on the student record with tag `lesson-credit`.

procedures.body:
# Lesson cancellation and make-up credit
When to use: Use when a family cancels a lesson or asks for a lesson to be credited or made up.

Background: Lessons are teachers' booked time, and families' lives are unpredictable, so cancellations and make-up requests are a regular part of running a music school. The difficulty is that handling them informally leads to inconsistency: one family receives a favour another was refused, teachers are unsure whether they are being paid for a gap, and records of who is owed what become muddled. This breeds resentment, disputes and extra administration. Families deserve a fair, predictable answer, and teachers deserve clarity about their schedules. This procedure exists so requests are treated evenly, recorded properly and resolved in a way that is understood by everyone involved.

Steps
1. [advisory] Open the student's record and the lesson time.
2. [advisory] Notice of 24 hours or more before the lesson: add one make-up credit (record_update the student's `makeup_credits` to the new total).
3. [advisory] Notice of less than 24 hours: no credit, unless the student was ill and a medical certificate is provided.
4. [advisory] Draft a reply to the family explaining the outcome, including the 24-hour notice rule when no credit is given, and how to book a make-up.
5. [advisory] Log a note on the student record with tag `lesson-credit`.

Never:
- Refund lesson fees for a single missed lesson.

Notes:
- Teachers are paid for late cancellations, which is why the 24-hour rule exists.

procedures.when_to_use: Use when a student, parent or customer complains about our service, a staff member or their experience.
procedures.title: Customer or family complaint
example_requests: a parent is unhappy with how lessons have been going
someone wrote in angry about how they were treated

steps.text: Create an incident record (record_create kind=incident) with type `complaint`, the complainant and a factual summary.
Draft an acknowledgement to the complainant within one business day: thank them, say the partner will follow up within 3 business days, no admission of fault, and no details about any staff member.
Create a task for the partner titled "Complaint: <name>" due 3 business days from today.
Log a note on the incident with tag `complaint`.

procedures.body:
# Customer or family complaint
When to use: Use when a student, parent or customer complains about our service, a staff member or their experience.

Background: A complaint is often the only moment a customer or family tells us directly that something went wrong, and how it is handled usually matters more than the original problem. Across the landscaping, bakery and music school businesses, complaints can reach any staff member, who may react defensively, make promises they cannot keep, or let the issue fade without follow-up. Left unmanaged, small frustrations become lost clients, public criticism and strained staff relationships. Complaints also reveal patterns the owners would otherwise never see. This procedure exists so every concern is heard respectfully, recorded, handled fairly and learned from, protecting both the people raising it and the reputation of the business.

Steps
1. [advisory] Create an incident record (record_create kind=incident) with type `complaint`, the complainant and a factual summary.
2. [advisory] Draft an acknowledgement to the complainant within one business day: thank them, say the partner will follow up within 3 business days, no admission of fault, and no details about any staff member.
3. [advisory] Create a task for the partner titled "Complaint: <name>" due 3 business days from today.
4. [advisory] Log a note on the incident with tag `complaint`.

Never:
- Share a staff member's personal details, roster or disciplinary matters.
- Offer refunds or compensation.

Notes:
- Keep the acknowledgement short and warm; the partner handles the substance.

procedures.body:
# Term fee reminder
When to use: Use when a music school family has not paid term fees by the start of term.

Background: Term fees are what keep the music school running, covering teacher wages, rooms and administration. When payment is missing at the start of term, the gap is easy to ignore because lessons carry on and nobody wants an awkward conversation with a family. Yet unpaid fees quietly build up, strain cash flow and can leave the school carrying costs it has already committed to. Handled badly, reminders can also feel abrupt or accusatory, or be applied unevenly between families. Often the cause is simply an oversight. This procedure exists so follow-up is polite, consistent and timely, protecting both the school's finances and its good relationships with families.

Steps
1. [advisory] Check the family's account for the term.
2. [advisory] Draft a reminder with the term fee amount and the school's payment options.
3. [advisory] If fees are unpaid by week 3, create a task for the school coordinator to call.
4. [advisory] Log a note on the family record with tag `fee-remind`.

procedures.body:
# Student withdrawal
When to use: Use when a student is leaving the music school permanently.

Background: When a student leaves the music school for good, the departure can be handled loosely because the family has already moved on. That is when loose ends appear: outstanding fees, unused credits, ongoing bookings, teacher schedules that still count the student, and records that are left out of date. Poor handling can also leave a family with a sour final impression, even after years of happy lessons. Careful exits protect the school's finances, keep its information accurate and free up teaching time for others. This procedure exists so departures are closed off tidily and courteously, and so the school learns why students leave and keeps the door open for their return.

Steps
1. [advisory] Confirm the last lesson date and any notice period owed.
2. [advisory] Set the enrolment status to `withdrawn`.
3. [advisory] Offer the freed slot to the first student on the waitlist for that instrument.
4. [advisory] Draft a farewell message.
5. [advisory] Log a note on the enrolment with tag `withdraw`.

procedures.when_to_use: Use when a staff member asks for annual leave or other time off.
procedures.title: Staff leave request
example_requests: one of the team wants a week off next month
someone asked for holidays

steps.text: Open the staff member's record for their leave balance and the leave request record.
Check the roster for the requested dates (records_search kind=roster): at least 2 other staff must remain rostered on each day.

If the balance covers every day and cover is met, set the leave request's status to `approved` (record_update). Otherwise create a task for the owner titled "Leave decision: <name>" with the reason, and leave the request pending.
Draft a reply to the staff member with the outcome (approved, or passed to the owner).
Log a note on the staff record with tag `leave`.

procedures.body:
# Staff leave request
When to use: Use when a staff member asks for annual leave or other time off.

Background: Time off affects everyone in a small team, not just the person asking. Marrowbank crews, Copperleaf counter and kitchen shifts, and Tidewell teaching timetables all rely on enough people being present to serve customers and students properly. Without a consistent way of handling leave requests, the business ends up with clashes where too many people are away together, jobs and lessons left uncovered, and last-minute scrambling. Staff can also feel treated unfairly when similar requests get different answers depending on who they asked or when. A clear, shared approach protects service to customers, keeps decisions fair and transparent, and ensures leave entitlements are recorded accurately so that nobody is surprised later by a dispute about what was agreed.

Steps
1. [advisory] Open the staff member's record for their leave balance and the leave request record.
2. [advisory] Check the roster for the requested dates (records_search kind=roster): at least 2 other staff must remain rostered on each day.
3. [advisory] If the balance covers every day and cover is met, set the leave request's status to `approved` (record_update). Otherwise create a task for the owner titled "Leave decision: <name>" with the reason, and leave the request pending.
4. [advisory] Draft a reply to the staff member with the outcome (approved, or passed to the owner).
5. [advisory] Log a note on the staff record with tag `leave`.

Done when: Request approved or with the owner, reply drafted, note logged.

Never:
- Promise unpaid leave or leave in advance: that is the owner's decision.

Notes:
- Count working days only; public holidays are not deducted.

procedures.when_to_use: Use when a new employee has accepted a job and is about to start.

example_requests: we've hired someone and they start next week
a new team member is joining

steps.text: Create a task for the bookkeeper to collect the tax file number declaration and super choice form before the first pay run.

Role checks: a music teacher needs a Working With Children Check number recorded before their first lesson (task for the school coordinator); bakery staff need a food handler certificate (task for the bakehouse manager); landscaping staff need a construction induction card (task for the landscapes lead).
Draft a welcome email to the new starter with their first day, start time, address and who to ask for.
Add a calendar entry for their induction on the first day (calendar_add).
Log a note on the staff record with tag `onboard`.

procedures.body:
# New staff onboarding
When to use: Use when a new employee has accepted a job and is about to start.

Background: The period between a person accepting a job and starting work is easy to neglect, yet it shapes how they feel about the business and how quickly they become useful. Without a proper process, new starters arrive to find nothing ready, no one expecting them, and paperwork half finished. Pay can be set up incorrectly, safety and food handling expectations can go unexplained, and the person may feel unwelcome or uncertain about what is asked of them. Mistakes made in the first days can also create risks for customers, students and colleagues. A consistent approach to preparing for a new employee means every business in the group gives a good first impression, meets its obligations as an employer, and helps people settle in with confidence.

Steps
1. [advisory] Create a task for the bookkeeper to collect the tax file number declaration and super choice form before the first pay run.
2. [advisory] Role checks: a music teacher needs a Working With Children Check number recorded before their first lesson (task for the school coordinator); bakery staff need a food handler certificate (task for the bakehouse manager); landscaping staff need a construction induction card (task for the landscapes lead).
3. [advisory] Draft a welcome email to the new starter with their first day, start time, address and who to ask for.
4. [advisory] Add a calendar entry for their induction on the first day (calendar_add).
5. [advisory] Log a note on the staff record with tag `onboard`.

Never:
- Ask for bank details or identity documents by email.

procedures.when_to_use: Use when a staff member says their pay or recorded hours are wrong.
procedures.title: Timesheet or pay hours query
example_requests: an employee reckons they were short-changed on hours
staff member questioning their pay

steps.text: Open the timesheet for the pay period and the clock-in record (records_get on both).
Compare the paid hours with the clocked hours.
If they differ, create a task for the bookkeeper titled "Pay adjustment: <name>" stating the exact difference in hours. If they match, no task.
Draft a reply to the staff member explaining what was found.
Log a note on the staff record with tag `timesheet`.

procedures.body:
# Timesheet or pay hours query
When to use: Use when a staff member says their pay or recorded hours are wrong.

Background: Pay is one of the most sensitive parts of working life, and people notice quickly when it looks wrong. When a staff member raises a concern about their hours or pay and there is no agreed way to handle it, the matter can drift, get passed between managers, or be brushed off. That leaves the person out of pocket or worried, damages trust, and can turn a simple recording mistake into a formal complaint. Unresolved errors also tend to repeat and can cause problems with the business's own records and legal obligations as an employer. Having a clear way to deal with these queries means concerns are taken seriously, fixed fairly and documented, and underlying causes are spotted and corrected.

Steps
1. [advisory] Open the timesheet for the pay period and the clock-in record (records_get on both).
2. [advisory] Compare the paid hours with the clocked hours.
3. [advisory] If they differ, create a task for the bookkeeper titled "Pay adjustment: <name>" stating the exact difference in hours. If they match, no task.
4. [advisory] Draft a reply to the staff member explaining what was found.
5. [advisory] Log a note on the staff record with tag `timesheet`.

Never:
- Change pay rates or make the adjustment yourself.

procedures.when_to_use: Use when an employee resigns or their employment ends.
procedures.title: Staff departure
example_requests: someone handed in their resignation

steps.text: Record the final day and notice period.
Create a task for the bookkeeper for final pay including leave owed.
Create a task to remove system access and collect keys on the last day.
Log a note on the staff record with tag `offboard`.

procedures.body:
# Staff departure
When to use: Use when an employee resigns or their employment ends.

Background: When someone leaves, the business is still responsible for many things connected to them. Without a dependable process, loose ends are common: access to systems and premises stays open, keys and uniforms go missing, final pay and entitlements are miscalculated, and customers or students are not told who will look after them next. Knowledge held only in that person's head can disappear overnight. Departures also affect the team, and a messy exit can leave bad feeling or create disputes that are costly to settle. A consistent approach protects business and customer information, keeps the employer's legal duties in order, treats the departing person respectfully, and leaves the group in good standing with someone who may speak about it publicly.

Steps
1. [advisory] Record the final day and notice period.
2. [advisory] Create a task for the bookkeeper for final pay including leave owed.
3. [advisory] Create a task to remove system access and collect keys on the last day.
4. [advisory] Log a note on the staff record with tag `offboard`.

procedures.when_to_use: Use when two staff members want to swap shifts.
procedures.title: Roster shift swap
example_requests: two of the crew want to trade shifts

steps.text: Check both staff are qualified for each other's shifts.
Check neither goes over 38 hours that week.
Update the roster record.
Log a note on the roster with tag `roster-swap`.

procedures.body:
# Roster shift swap
When to use: Use when two staff members want to swap shifts.

Background: Shift swaps look simple, but when they are arranged informally between colleagues they regularly cause trouble. The manager may not know who is actually working, so a site can be short of skills or licences needed for the day, or a lesson or service goes uncovered. Swaps can also quietly lead to people working more than is safe or fair, create pay mistakes when hours do not match what was recorded, and cause arguments if one person later says the arrangement was never agreed. Having a shared way of handling swaps lets staff enjoy flexibility while the business keeps accurate rosters, maintains proper coverage and keeps everyone paid correctly for the work done.

Steps
1. [advisory] Check both staff are qualified for each other's shifts.
2. [advisory] Check neither goes over 38 hours that week.
3. [advisory] Update the roster record.
4. [advisory] Log a note on the roster with tag `roster-swap`.

procedures.when_to_use: Use when a piece of business equipment breaks down or stops working properly.
procedures.title: Equipment fault
example_requests: one of our machines has stopped working
the gear broke down on the job

steps.text: Find the asset record (records_search kind=asset) and check its warranty or service-contract fields.
Set the asset's status to `out_of_service` (record_update).

If the asset is under warranty or a service contract, draft the fault report to the provider named on the asset record, not to a general repairer. If not, create a task for the business's manager to get a repair quote.
Create a task for the business's manager to arrange a workaround while the asset is out.
Log a note on the asset with tag `fault` describing the symptom.

procedures.body:
# Equipment fault
When to use: Use when a piece of business equipment breaks down or stops working properly.

Background: Mowers, ovens, coffee machines, pianos and the other equipment across the group are essential to earning a living and serving customers. When something fails and there is no common way of dealing with it, problems are often ignored, worked around or reported to no one. Small faults then grow into costly breakdowns, and a damaged or unreliable item can become a danger to staff, customers or students. Work gets delayed, food or services suffer, and nobody can tell whether the same issue has happened before or whether a repair or warranty is involved. A clear approach ensures faults are noticed, made safe, passed to the right person and recorded so that the business can limit disruption and expense.

Steps
1. [advisory] Find the asset record (records_search kind=asset) and check its warranty or service-contract fields.
2. [advisory] Set the asset's status to `out_of_service` (record_update).
3. [advisory] If the asset is under warranty or a service contract, draft the fault report to the provider named on the asset record, not to a general repairer. If not, create a task for the business's manager to get a repair quote.
4. [advisory] Create a task for the business's manager to arrange a workaround while the asset is out.
5. [advisory] Log a note on the asset with tag `fault` describing the symptom.

Done when: Asset marked out of service, warranty provider contacted or quote task created, workaround task, note logged.

Never:
- Book or pay for a repair yourself.

Notes:
- Warranty work done by a third party can void the warranty.
- Describe the symptom exactly as reported; do not guess the cause.

procedures.when_to_use: Use when someone is injured, or nearly injured, at work or on one of our sites.
procedures.title: Safety incident report
example_requests: someone got hurt at work today
a visitor had a fall on site

steps.text: Create an incident record (record_create kind=incident) with type `safety`: who, where, when, what happened and the injury.
Create a task for the partner to review the incident within 24 hours.
If the injury needed hospital treatment (or involves a fracture, burns needing a doctor, or a head injury), create a task for the owner titled "Notifiable incident: notify the regulator today".
Log a note on the incident with tag `whs`.

procedures.body:
# Safety incident report
When to use: Use when someone is injured, or nearly injured, at work or on one of our sites.

Background: Injuries and close calls are warnings about how work is really being done. In a group that includes outdoor landscaping, hot kitchens and teaching spaces, hazards are real. Without a dependable way of responding and recording what happened, people receive inconsistent care, near misses are shrugged off, and the same hazard injures someone else later. Poor records can also leave the business exposed when insurers, regulators or injured people ask questions, and can undermine the confidence of staff who need to know that their wellbeing matters. Treating every incident and near miss seriously ensures people are looked after, causes are understood and fixed, and the business meets its legal and moral duties.

Steps
1. [advisory] Create an incident record (record_create kind=incident) with type `safety`: who, where, when, what happened and the injury.
2. [advisory] Create a task for the partner to review the incident within 24 hours.
3. [advisory] If the injury needed hospital treatment (or involves a fracture, burns needing a doctor, or a head injury), create a task for the owner titled "Notifiable incident: notify the regulator today".
4. [advisory] Log a note on the incident with tag `whs`.

Never:
- Admit liability in any message.

Notes:
- Notifiable incidents must be reported to the regulator immediately; the owner does this.

procedures.when_to_use: Use when personal information may have gone to the wrong person, been lost, or been seen by someone who should not have it.
procedures.title: Privacy incident triage
example_requests: we accidentally sent someone else's details to the wrong person
a list with people's info went to the wrong email

steps.text: Contain it: create a task for the staff member's manager (or the sender's role) to ask the recipient to delete the information and confirm they have.
Create an incident record (record_create kind=incident) with type `privacy`: what information, whose, how many people, how it happened.
If health, financial or identity information is involved, or more than 10 people are affected, create a task for the owner titled "Privacy breach assessment (30-day clock)".
Log a note on the incident with tag `privacy`.

procedures.body:
# Privacy incident triage
When to use: Use when personal information may have gone to the wrong person, been lost, or been seen by someone who should not have it.

Background: The group holds personal details about customers, students, parents and staff, and people trust us to look after them. Mistakes happen, such as a message sent to the wrong person, a lost device or a document left where others can see it. Without a clear way to assess these situations, they are often hidden out of embarrassment, handled by whoever notices, or judged inconsistently. Delay and silence can make the harm worse for the people affected and may breach legal duties to notify. A shared approach helps the business work out quickly how serious a situation is, limit the damage, treat affected people fairly and learn from what went wrong so it is less likely to recur.

Steps
1. [advisory] Contain it: create a task for the staff member's manager (or the sender's role) to ask the recipient to delete the information and confirm they have.
2. [advisory] Create an incident record (record_create kind=incident) with type `privacy`: what information, whose, how many people, how it happened.
3. [advisory] If health, financial or identity information is involved, or more than 10 people are affected, create a task for the owner titled "Privacy breach assessment (30-day clock)".
4. [advisory] Log a note on the incident with tag `privacy`.

Done when: Containment task, incident record, owner task when serious, note logged; no messages to affected people.

Never:
- Contact the affected people before the owner has decided how to notify them.

Notes:
- The 30-day assessment clock starts when we become aware.
- Allergy and medical notes count as health information.

procedures.when_to_use: Use when a fridge, cool room or hot-hold unit has been outside safe food temperatures.
procedures.title: Food temperature breach
example_requests: the cold room was warm overnight

steps.text: Record the temperatures and how long the food was outside 5-60 degrees.
Under 2 hours: use or refrigerate; 2-4 hours: use immediately; over 4 hours: discard and log the waste.
Create a task for the bakehouse manager to check the unit.
Log a note on the food safety log with tag `food-temp`.

procedures.body:
# Food temperature breach
When to use: Use when a fridge, cool room or hot-hold unit has been outside safe food temperatures.

Background: Food that has spent time outside safe temperatures can look and smell perfectly normal while carrying bacteria that make customers seriously ill. A cafe's reputation, licence and legal standing all depend on preventing that. When a fridge, cool room or hot-hold unit drifts out of range and there is no agreed response, staff are left guessing. Some throw out good stock needlessly, while others keep serving food that should have been discarded because they are worried about the cost or wastage. Equipment problems may also go unreported and recur. Having a consistent procedure protects customers, supports proper judgement about affected food, creates a record to show inspectors, and helps identify and fix the underlying equipment fault.

Steps
1. [advisory] Record the temperatures and how long the food was outside 5-60 degrees.
2. [advisory] Under 2 hours: use or refrigerate; 2-4 hours: use immediately; over 4 hours: discard and log the waste.
3. [advisory] Create a task for the bakehouse manager to check the unit.
4. [advisory] Log a note on the food safety log with tag `food-temp`.

procedures.when_to_use: Use for the monthly review of online reviews and feedback forms.
procedures.title: Customer feedback review
example_requests: summarise what customers said about us this month

steps.text: Collect the month's reviews and feedback forms.
Group them by theme.
Draft a one-page summary for the partner.
Log a note on the feedback log with tag `feedback`.

procedures.body:
# Customer feedback review
When to use: Use for the monthly review of online reviews and feedback forms.

Background: Online reviews and feedback forms are some of the most honest information the group receives about how customers and students experience our businesses. If nobody looks at them regularly, praise goes unacknowledged, genuine complaints sit unanswered in public view, and recurring problems stay hidden until they cost real business. Responses written in a hurry or by different people can also sound inconsistent or defensive. A regular review gives the group a steady habit of listening, so that patterns across Marrowbank, Copperleaf and Tidewell become visible, good work is recognised, and issues are passed to the right people to act on. It also shows the community that the business cares what they think.

Steps
1. [advisory] Collect the month's reviews and feedback forms.
2. [advisory] Group them by theme.
3. [advisory] Draft a one-page summary for the partner.
4. [advisory] Log a note on the feedback log with tag `feedback`.

procedures.when_to_use: Use when a customer wants a price for landscaping or garden construction work.

procedures.body:
# Landscaping quote preparation
When to use: Use when a customer wants a price for landscaping or garden construction work.

Background: Customers choose a landscaper largely on the price they are given, so a quote is both a sales document and a promise. Without a consistent way of preparing it, quotes tend to leave out materials, labour or site difficulties, and the business ends up absorbing the cost or having an awkward conversation once work has begun. Vague descriptions of what is and is not included lead to disputes about what the customer thought they were buying. Quotes that differ from one job to the next also make it hard to compare results and learn which work actually earns money. A steady approach protects margins, sets honest expectations from the first conversation and gives the customer a clear document they can trust.

Steps
1. [advisory] Open the site visit notes (records_search kind=site_visit) and the current rate card RC-ML-2026 (records_get).
2. [advisory] Price each item from the rate card. Add a 10% contingency on earthworks and excavation lines only.
3. [advisory] Quotes are valid for 30 days from today.
4. [advisory] Create a quote record (record_create kind=quote) with the lines, the total including contingency and `valid_until`.
5. [advisory] Draft the quote to the customer (never send it).
6. [advisory] Log a note on the quote with tag `quote-prep`.

Done when: Quote record with correct total and validity, draft to the customer, note logged.

Never:
- Discount or round down rate-card prices.

Notes:
- Prices on RC-ML-2026 include GST.
- Measurements come from the site visit notes, not from the customer's message.

procedures.body:
# Job variation
When to use: Use when a customer asks for a change to a landscaping job that is already under way.

Background: Once a landscaping job is under way, customers often think of new ideas or change their minds when they see the work taking shape. Without a clear procedure, these changes get agreed casually on site, and nobody is quite sure afterwards what was promised or what it should cost. The business can end up doing extra work for free, the customer can be surprised by a bigger bill, and the crew can be left working to different instructions. Changes can also disturb the order of work and the arrangements already made with suppliers and others. Handling variations properly keeps everyone clear about the current scope, protects the relationship and ensures extra effort is fairly paid for.

Steps
1. [advisory] Open the job record and the rate card RC-ML-2026.
2. [advisory] Price the change from the rate card.
3. [advisory] Draft a written variation to the customer with the description and price, for their signature before any extra work starts.
4. [advisory] Set the job's `status` to `variation_pending` (record_update).
5. [advisory] Log a note on the job with tag `variation`.

Never:
- Start or schedule the extra work before the variation is signed.

# Job completion and handover
When to use: Use when a landscaping job is finished and has to be handed over to the customer.

Background: The end of a landscaping job is the moment the customer judges the whole experience, and it is easy to get wrong when the crew is keen to move on. Without a proper handover, small unfinished items are missed, the site may be left untidy, and the customer may not know how to care for new plants, lawns or features. Disagreements about whether the work matches what was agreed tend to surface later, when they are harder to resolve. Unclear closure can also delay payment and weaken the chance of repeat work or referrals. A deliberate handover confirms the job is truly complete, leaves the customer informed and confident, and gives the business a clean finish.

Steps
1. [advisory] Open the job record for the contract price, deposit paid and final inspection result.
2. [advisory] Create a task for the bookkeeper titled "Final invoice: <job>" with the balance owing (contract price minus deposit paid).
3. [advisory] Draft a handover message to the customer with the plant care guide link and our 12-month workmanship warranty.
4. [advisory] Set the job's `status` to `completed` (record_update).
5. [advisory] Log a note on the job with tag `handover`.

Never:
- Issue the invoice yourself.

# Site visit booking
When to use: Use when a new enquiry needs a site visit booked to measure up.

Background: A site visit is usually the first time the business sees the customer's property, and good quotes depend on what is learned there. Without a reliable way of booking it, enquiries wait too long, visits clash with other commitments, and staff turn up without the right information or access. Customers who feel ignored or confused at this early stage often go to a competitor. Poorly arranged visits also waste travel and staff time, and can result in missed measurements or unanswered questions that force a second trip. Booking visits carefully makes a good first impression, ensures the right person attends prepared, and gives the business the details it needs to price the work accurately.

When to use: Use when we need to bring in a subcontractor (electrician, plumber, concreter) for a job.

Background: Some landscaping work needs specialist trades such as electrical, plumbing or concrete, and the business relies on these outside people to meet the same standard as its own crew. Without a consistent approach to bringing them in, problems appear: work is done to an unclear brief, trades arrive at the wrong stage, costs are not agreed beforehand, and responsibility for mistakes is uncertain. There are also risks around qualifications, insurance and safety that the business remains answerable for to the customer. Poor coordination can hold up the whole job and damage the company's reputation. A clear procedure keeps expectations aligned, protects the business and customer, and helps specialist work fit smoothly into the project.

Steps

lay out the choices for the boss

procedures.body:
# Decision brief for the owner
When to use: Use when the owner has to make a decision and needs the options laid out first.

Background: The owner has many demands on their attention and is often asked to decide things across several businesses. When a question reaches them without background, they must stop and chase missing facts, or they decide on partial information and later regret it. Options may be presented in an unbalanced way, with the preferred answer pushed and the risks left out. Decisions can then be delayed, reversed or made without understanding the consequences. A well-prepared brief respects the owner's time by setting out what needs deciding, the realistic choices and what each would mean, so that the decision is made confidently, can be explained later and does not need to be revisited.

Steps
1. [advisory] Gather the facts from the relevant records (quotes, figures, constraints).
2. [advisory] Write the brief: the question, 2-3 options each with cost and main risk, a recommendation, and which options are one-way doors (hard or costly to reverse).
3. [advisory] Create a decision record (record_create kind=decision) with status `awaiting_owner` containing the brief.
4. [advisory] Create a task for the owner titled "Decision needed: <topic>" referring to the decision record.
5. [advisory] Log a note on the decision record with tag `decision`.

Done when: Decision record awaiting the owner, task for the owner, note logged; nothing acted on.

Never:
- Act on any option, contact suppliers to accept, or commit spending.

Notes:
- Name one-way doors explicitly; the owner wants to know what cannot be undone.
- Use the figures in the records, not estimates.

procedures.body:
# Task handoff
When to use: Use when a piece of unfinished work passes from one person to another.

Background: Work regularly passes from one person to another because of leave, changing workloads or shifts in responsibility. Without a careful handoff, the person taking over inherits a half-finished task with no understanding of what has been done, what is outstanding or what has been promised to customers or colleagues. Things get repeated, dropped or done differently from what was agreed, and customers notice the confusion. The person leaving may also be repeatedly interrupted with questions. A good handoff keeps momentum, protects commitments already made, saves effort and makes sure that responsibility for the work is clearly understood by everyone involved.

Steps
1. [advisory] Open the work record and read its progress.
2. [advisory] Write the handoff: a summary of where it is, decisions made, and the remaining work, marking every item [done], [checked] or [assumed].
3. [advisory] Log the handoff as a note on the work record with tag `handoff`.

Never:
- Hand work to someone outside the business it belongs to.

- [assumed] marks anything not verified; the receiver checks those first.

procedures.body:
# Weekly owner brief
When to use: Use when the owner asks for the regular round-up of how the businesses stand.

Background: The owner oversees a landscaping firm, a bakery cafe and a music school, and cannot be present in each one daily. Without a regular round-up, they learn about problems late, hear news unevenly from whoever happens to speak up, and find it hard to see how the businesses compare or where attention is needed. Good news can go unnoticed while small issues quietly grow. Reports produced in different styles also make it hard to spot patterns from one period to the next. A consistent round-up gives the owner a dependable picture of how each business stands, supports earlier and better decisions, and reduces the need for scattered questions and updates.

Steps
1. [advisory] Find obligations due in the next 7 days (records_search kind=obligation).
2. [advisory] Find overdue customer invoices and total them (records_search kind=invoice).
3. [advisory] Find open incidents (records_search kind=incident).

5. [advisory] Draft the brief to the owner's email with four headed sections in this order: Obligations, Overdue invoices, Incidents, Cash.
6. [advisory] Log a note on the BRIEF-LOG record with tag `weekly-brief`.

Never:
- Include staff personal matters in the brief.

# Meeting minutes
When to use: Use when notes from a meeting need to be written up as minutes with actions.

Background: Meetings only matter if what was discussed and agreed is remembered afterwards. Without written minutes, people leave with different understandings of what was decided, and actions are forgotten or assumed to belong to someone else. Absent colleagues are left uninformed, and the same topics are raised again because nobody can show what was already settled. When disagreements arise later, there is no reliable record to refer to. Properly written minutes capture the decisions and who is responsible for each action, give everyone a shared account, and turn conversation into follow-through so that the time spent in the meeting is not wasted.

Steps
1. [advisory] List attendees, decisions and actions with owners and dates.
2. [advisory] Create a task for each action.
3. [advisory] Draft the minutes to the attendees.
4. [advisory] Log a note on the meeting record with tag `minutes`.

procedures.body:
# Standing rule change request
When to use: Use when someone wants to change one of the business's standing rules or limits.

Background: The businesses run on standing rules and limits that exist for good reasons, often learned from past mistakes, such as protecting money, safety, customers or quality. Without a proper way to propose changes, rules get quietly bent, ignored or altered by whoever is under pressure at the time. Different people then follow different versions, and the original purpose is lost. Changes made casually can also create risks nobody thought through. A clear request process makes sure the reasons for a change are considered, the right person approves it, and everyone is told, so the rules stay trusted, consistent and suited to how the business actually works.

Steps
1. [advisory] Record the proposed change as a proposal record (record_create kind=rule_proposal).
2. [advisory] Create a task for the owner to approve or reject.

# Raising a purchase order
When to use: Use before ordering goods or materials from a supplier, to raise a purchase order first.

Background: Buying on a handshake or a quick phone call feels efficient, but it leaves the business with no clear record of what was agreed before the money is committed. Without a purchase order raised first, the same item gets ordered twice by different people, prices drift from what was quoted, and nobody can say who approved the spend. When the delivery and the supplier's bill arrive, there is nothing to check them against, so disputes drag on and mistakes get paid. A purchase order raised ahead of the order gives Marrowbank Landscapes, Copperleaf Bakehouse and Tidewell Music School a shared, checkable record of what was wanted, from whom, and on what terms.

Steps
1. [advisory] Check the supplier is on the approved supplier list.
2. [advisory] Create a purchase order record with items, quantities and agreed prices.
3. [advisory] Orders over $2,000 need a partner task for approval before sending.
