# New supplier set-up
When to use: Use when we start buying from a supplier we have never used before.

Background: Every new supplier is a new way for money to leave the business, so it matters that we know who we are dealing with before the first payment. Without a proper set-up, details get taken from an email or a bill and never checked, which opens the door to fraud, payments sent to the wrong account, and tax or compliance gaps that surface months later. Incomplete records also mean the finance team chases basic information every time something goes wrong. A consistent set-up gives each supplier one trusted record, keeps our dealings with them clear, and protects all three businesses from paying people we cannot properly identify.

Steps
1. [advisory] Collect the supplier's ABN and check it is active.
2. [advisory] Collect bank details on the supplier's letterhead and verify them by phone.
3. [advisory] Create the supplier record with payment terms.
4. [advisory] Log a note on the main record with tag `supplier-new`.

When to use: Use when a staff member paid for something for the business out of their own pocket and wants it back.

Background: Staff sometimes cover a business cost personally because it is quick or urgent, and the business needs to repay them fairly and accurately. Without a clear approach, claims arrive late, with missing receipts or vague descriptions, and the finance team cannot tell what was bought or whether it was for the business at all. Staff can wait too long to be repaid, which breeds frustration, while the business risks paying for private spending or paying twice for the same item. A consistent way of handling these claims keeps reimbursement fair, protects the business's records and tax position, and treats the people who have helped us out with respect.

Steps

# Duplicate bill check
When to use: Use when a supplier bill looks like it may already have been entered or paid once before.

Background: Suppliers resend bills, reminders get mistaken for new invoices, and the same charge can reach us by post, email and a statement. When a bill looks familiar, the easy mistake is to enter it or pay it again. Duplicate payments waste cash, and recovering them from a supplier can be slow and awkward, sometimes leaving the business out of pocket for a long while. They also distort our costs and make the books harder to trust. Taking care to check whether a bill has already been dealt with protects our money, keeps supplier relationships on good terms, and keeps our financial records accurate.

Steps

2. [advisory] If a duplicate exists, set the newer bill's status to `duplicate`.

# Direct debit set-up
When to use: Use when a supplier or service wants to collect payments from us by direct debit.

Background: A direct debit lets a supplier take money from our account without asking each time, which is convenient but carries real risk. Without care at the start, we can agree to collections we did not intend, give the wrong person authority, or lose track of what is leaving the account and why. Amounts can change quietly, payments can continue after a service has ended, and cancelling later can be frustrating. Because the money moves automatically, mistakes are often noticed only after the damage is done. A careful, consistent set-up keeps control of the bank account with the business and ensures every automatic payment is understood, approved and recorded.

Steps

When to use: Use when a supplier announces that its prices or rates will go up from a future date.

Without a considered response, the business absorbs the increase without noticing, margins shrink, and we miss the chance to question the change, compare alternatives or adjust our own prices. This matters in a landscaping firm, a bakery and a music school alike, where small cost shifts add up. Reviewing each announcement gives us time to decide how to respond, keeps the right people informed, and ensures we are making a deliberate choice about whom we buy from rather than drifting into higher costs.

Steps
1. [advisory] Record the new prices and effective date on the supplier's rate card record.
2. [advisory] Estimate the yearly cost impact from last year's purchases.

# Petty cash count
When to use: Use for the monthly count of the petty cash tin at a business.

Background: Cash kept on the premises is easy to spend and easy to lose track of. Small purchases without receipts, money borrowed and not returned, and honest counting slips can all leave the tin out of step with the records. Left alone, the gap grows quietly until nobody can explain it, which breeds suspicion between colleagues and makes genuine errors hard to trace. Regularly counting the tin and comparing it with what was recorded keeps problems small and easy to explain, protects staff from unfair doubt, and shows that the business looks after its cash with the same care it gives money in the bank.

Steps
1. [advisory] Count the cash and total the receipts.
2. [advisory] Compare with the float.
3. [advisory] Record any difference on the petty cash record.

When to use: Use at month end to list goods received but not yet billed.

Background: Goods often arrive before the supplier's bill does, so at the end of a month the business has received something it has not yet been charged for. If those items are left out, the costs appear in the wrong month, profits look better than they really are, and the following month takes an unexpected hit. Managers then make decisions on figures that do not reflect reality. Listing what has been received but not yet billed gives a more honest picture of what each business actually spent, makes monthly results comparable, and avoids unpleasant surprises when late bills finally turn up.

Steps

procedures.body:
# Customer credit account application
When to use: Use when a business customer asks to buy on account instead of paying upfront.

Background: Letting a business customer buy now and pay later is a form of lending, and the risk sits with us. Without a proper look at who is asking, we may extend credit to customers who are slow to pay or never pay, leaving us short of cash to cover wages, ingredients and materials. Informal promises also create confusion about what was agreed and who is responsible for the debt. A consistent application process helps us offer credit fairly to customers who deserve it, sets expectations on both sides from the outset, and protects the business from avoidable bad debts and awkward collection conversations.

Steps

A child's photo might then appear in a newsletter, on social media or on a noticeboard against the family's wishes. That can cause real distress, damage relationships, and raise privacy concerns for the school. This procedure exists so a family's latest choice is clearly recorded, reliably respected and easy to confirm.

As that period draws to a close, the decision about what happens next carries real weight for the person and for the team. Without a proper review, the end of probation can slip past unnoticed, leaving the employee uncertain about their standing and the manager with no record of how they performed. Feedback may be vague, concerns may be raised too late to act on, and good people may feel overlooked. Decisions made without a clear, fair conversation can also create disputes. This procedure keeps the review honest, documented and respectful to everyone involved.

# Working With Children Check renewal

These checks do not last forever, and it is easy for a renewal to be forgotten amid busy teaching schedules. If one lapses unnoticed, a teacher may be working without valid clearance, which exposes children to avoidable risk and the school to serious legal and reputational consequences. Last-minute scrambles also disrupt lessons and put stress on staff. This procedure exists so that upcoming expiries are noticed early, handled calmly and recorded clearly, keeping children protected and the school in good standing at all times.

# Staff training record

Background: Courses and certifications matter to the group, whether they relate to food safety, first aid, equipment operation or teaching practice. They show that staff are capable, and some are needed to meet legal or insurance obligations. When a staff member finishes training and nobody records it, the evidence goes missing. Certificates end up in personal inboxes, renewals are forgotten, and managers cannot tell who is qualified for which tasks. During an audit, an incident or an insurance query, the business may struggle to prove that its people were properly trained. Staff also lose credit for their effort. This procedure keeps a reliable, central record of completed training so skills are visible and recognised.

Steps

# Weekly roster publication

When publication is rushed, inconsistent or unclear, people turn up on the wrong day, shifts go uncovered, and customers or students are let down. Staff also need reasonable notice to organise their lives outside work, and confusion about the roster quickly erodes goodwill. Different versions circulating among staff make matters worse. This procedure exists so that the finalised roster reaches everyone in a dependable, recognisable way each week, and so people can trust that what they receive is accurate and current.

# Overtime approval

Background: Sometimes a business needs people to work beyond their rostered hours, whether because of a busy period, a staff shortage or an unexpected job. Extra hours cost money, affect wages and can tire people out, so they should never be arranged casually. Without a clear approval process, staff may work extra time that nobody expected, managers may promise hours they cannot budget for, and pay disputes can follow. Fatigue also raises safety risks, especially in landscaping and kitchen work. Unrecorded overtime makes payroll errors likely. This procedure exists so extra hours are agreed openly, fairly and in a way that protects both the employee and the business.

Steps

# Staff grievance
When to use: Use when an employee raises a formal complaint about a colleague or their treatment at work.

Background: When an employee raises a formal complaint about a colleague or about how they have been treated, they are placing considerable trust in the business. How that complaint is handled affects the person's wellbeing, the team's morale and the business's legal standing. Without a consistent process, complaints can be brushed aside, handled by someone with a conflict of interest, or discussed too widely. People may feel unheard or fear retaliation, and small problems can grow into resignations, disputes or claims. Fairness to the person accused matters just as much. This procedure exists so every grievance is taken seriously, treated confidentially and dealt with fairly, with a clear record of what was done.

Steps

If issuing gear is left to chance, people end up working without proper protection, wearing worn or ill-fitting items, or waiting too long for replacements. Stock is lost or handed out inconsistently, and the business cannot show it met its safety duties after an injury. This procedure exists so that every staff member is properly equipped, items are accounted for, and safety and professionalism are maintained across all three businesses.

# Payroll detail change

Background: Pay details are sensitive and errors are costly. When a staff member wants to change their tax information, super fund or bank details, the business must be sure the request is genuine and the update is accurate. Without a careful process, wages can be paid to the wrong account, tax can be withheld incorrectly, and super contributions can go to a fund the employee no longer uses. Fraudsters also impersonate staff to redirect pay. Mistakes upset employees, create extra work to correct, and may lead to compliance problems. This procedure exists so that changes are made correctly, recorded properly and handled with the privacy that personal financial information deserves.

Steps

# Pest sighting
When to use: Use when pests (rodents, cockroaches) are seen in the bakehouse.

Pests are rarely a one-off: what is seen is usually a small part of a larger problem, and if it is ignored, brushed aside or handled differently by each person on shift, the problem grows, stock is contaminated and inspectors or customers may find it before we do. Without a shared procedure, sightings go unreported, staff assume someone else has dealt with it, and nothing is recorded to show we acted responsibly. This procedure exists so every sighting is taken seriously, handled consistently and documented, protecting our customers, our team and the bakehouse.

Steps

When the security company calls out of hours, the situation is uncertain: it may be a fault, a mistake or a genuine break-in. Without an agreed approach, people can be hard to reach, several staff may turn up unsure who is in charge, or no one may respond at all. Worse, someone could put themselves at risk by walking into a situation they do not understand. Confusion also leaves gaps in the record, which matters for insurance and for spotting repeat problems. This procedure exists so alarms are answered promptly, safely and consistently, and so that what happened is properly recorded.

Steps

In the stress of the moment, people forget what to gather, say things they should not, or fail to tell the business at all. Without a clear procedure, details are lost, insurance claims are delayed or weakened, and we may not learn of an incident until a third party contacts us. Inconsistent handling can also leave an injured person without proper support, or leave us exposed to disputes over fault. This procedure exists so that every accident is reported fully and promptly, people are looked after, and the business can respond properly to what follows.

# Lost property
When to use: Use when an item is left behind at the school or bakehouse.

Background: People leave things behind at the music school and the bakehouse all the time, from coats and keys to phones, instrument cases and wallets. To the owner these items can matter a great deal, and they may be worth real money or hold personal information. Without a consistent approach, items get moved around, thrown out, kept by whoever finds them or simply forgotten in a back room. Owners then struggle to get their belongings back, staff are unsure what they may do, and we risk complaints or accusations of carelessness or worse. This procedure exists so that left-behind items are treated fairly and consistently, can be matched with their owners, and are recorded so everyone can see what happened.

Steps

# Suspicious email or phishing
When to use: Use when a staff member receives a suspicious email or clicked a link they should not have.

Background: Our three businesses rely on email for customer bookings, supplier invoices, payments and staff communication, which makes it a favourite route for scammers. A convincing message can trick a busy person into clicking a link, opening a file or handing over a password. The real damage often comes afterwards, when someone realises their mistake but stays quiet out of embarrassment, giving criminals time to reach accounts, money and customer details. Without a shared procedure, suspicious messages are forwarded around, ignored or deleted, and we never learn that others were targeted. This procedure exists so staff feel safe raising a concern early, without blame, so we can limit harm and warn everyone else.

Steps

In a bakery, a school and a landscaping crew, cuts, burns, strains and bites are all realistic, and the person reaching for a kit is usually stressed and in a hurry. Without a regular check and a habit of replacing what has been used, kits quietly run short, supplies pass their useful life, and nobody notices until the moment of need. Each site then ends up in a different state, and staff cannot be sure what is available. This procedure exists so every kit is dependable, our duty of care is met, and our people can trust the help is there when it matters.

In the bakehouse, spills of liquids, oil and flour are routine, and customers at the school and cafe may not expect a hazard. Without a clear approach, people walk around a spill assuming someone else will deal with it, or the hazard is cleaned up without any warning or record. Falls cause real harm to customers and staff, and can lead to claims against us. This procedure exists so hazards are dealt with promptly and consistently, people are protected in the meantime, and we have a record that we took care.

Routine servicing keeps it safe, efficient and dependable, and prevents small wear from becoming costly failure. Without a shared process, servicing is easily put off because everyone is busy and nothing seems wrong, until a breakdown stops a bakery morning, a crew job or a lesson. Unserviced equipment can also become unsafe, may void warranties, and leaves us unable to show that we maintained it properly. This procedure exists so that servicing is handled consistently, nothing falls through the cracks, and records are kept so we know the condition and history of what we rely on.

This procedure exists so claims are handled fairly, consistently and with a clear record, and so we learn from what goes wrong.

Without a shared approach, preparation falls on whoever is available, work is duplicated or left to the last moment, and pricing and promises are not checked by the right people. We risk committing to something we cannot deliver, or being disqualified on a technicality. This procedure exists so that tender responses are prepared carefully, reviewed properly and presented consistently, giving us the best fair chance of winning work we can do well.

Customers may feel taken for granted, or be surprised by a change in price they never discussed. Weather, suppliers and other jobs all compete for the same people, so informal arrangements tend to unravel quickly. The result is missed start dates, rushed finishes, overtime and unhappy customers who start to doubt that we are organised. A consistent scheduling procedure keeps everyone working from the same picture, so promises made at the point of sale can actually be delivered.

When to use: Use before work starts on a site with excavation, retaining walls over 1 m or machinery.

# Writing a procedure test
When to use: Use when writing tests for a new or changed procedure.

Background: A procedure is only useful if it actually produces the right behaviour when real work is under way. When a procedure is new or has been changed, it is easy to assume it works because it reads well. Without proper tests, gaps stay hidden: instructions that are vague, situations nobody thought of, or changes that quietly break something that used to work. Staff at Marrowbank, Copperleaf and Tidewell then discover the problems in front of customers, when the cost is highest. This procedure exists so that tests are written thoughtfully, reflect realistic situations, and genuinely challenge the procedure rather than flattering it. Good tests give the group honest evidence that a procedure does what it claims.

2. [advisory] Write paraphrases without trigger words.

# Resuming from a checkpoint
When to use: Use when picking up an interrupted automated job.

Background: Automated jobs sometimes stop partway through, because of an outage, an error or a deliberate pause. The person picking the work up faces a tempting but risky choice: start over from the beginning, or guess where things left off. Starting over can duplicate work already done, such as sending messages twice or repeating changes, while guessing can leave gaps that nobody notices. Either way, the results become unreliable and hard to untangle. This procedure exists so that interrupted work is continued from a known, recorded position rather than from assumptions. Without it, the group risks double entries, missed items and confusion about what was actually finished, across all three businesses.

Steps
1. [advisory] Read the last checkpoint.
2. [advisory] Verify completed items.
3. [advisory] Continue from the first unverified item.

When to use: Use when measuring whether a change to a system or process actually helped.

Background: Groups often make a change to a system or process and then simply feel that it went well. Feelings can mislead: a busy week, a quiet week or an unrelated shift can make a change look better or worse than it really was. Without a fair way to judge, the group may keep something that does nothing, abandon something useful, or pile on further changes without knowing which one mattered. Time and goodwill are spent on effort that never pays back. This procedure exists so that the result of a change is judged honestly and against what was true before, giving Marrowbank, Copperleaf and Tidewell reliable evidence for deciding what to keep, adjust or drop.

When to use: Use before releasing a copy of information into a space other people can see.

Background: Putting a copy of information into a space that other people can see is easy to do and very hard to take back. A copy may include private details about customers, students, staff or suppliers that were never meant to be broadly seen, or it may be out of date by the time others rely on it. Problems then include privacy complaints, awkward conversations and decisions made on stale information. This procedure exists so that a careful check happens before anything becomes visible to others, protecting people's trust and the reputation of each business in the group.

When to use: Use when a supplier bill is to be paid or a payment for it prepared.

Background: Suppliers keep Marrowbank Landscapes, Copperleaf Bakehouse and Tidewell Music School running, and paying them is one of the most direct ways money leaves the business. Without a clear procedure, the same bill can be paid twice, a payment can go to the wrong account, or a charge can be settled without anyone checking that the goods or services were actually delivered as agreed. Errors like these are hard to recover once funds have moved, and they strain relationships with good suppliers. Mistakes can also come from fraudulent invoices that look genuine or from changed bank details that nobody confirmed. This procedure exists so that every payment is accurate, properly authorised and traceable, protecting cash, trust and the business's reputation.

How to run it: This action is gated in the brain. Start a run with procedures_start (procedure pay-supplier-bill@3, your task_id, action_class payment), submit each enforced step's evidence with procedures_check, and pass the receipt you receive to payments_prepare. The brain computes every check itself.

Steps
1. [enforced] c1 bill-matches-order: the bill total equals its purchase order total. Evidence: {"bill_id": ...}.
2. [enforced] c2 payee-bank-on-file: the bank details on the bill equal the supplier's bank details on file. Evidence: {"bill_id": ...}.
3. [enforced] c3 not-already-paid: no payment has been made for this bill. Evidence: {"bill_id": ...}.

- Pay to bank details that are not the supplier's details on file.

- Invoice fraud usually arrives as changed bank details on an otherwise normal invoice.

When to use: Use when an email or document is to be sent to someone outside the business.

Background: Anything sent from the business to an outside person speaks for the whole group, whether it reaches a customer, a supplier, a parent or a member of the public. Once an email or document leaves, it cannot be taken back. Without a shared procedure, messages can go to the wrong recipient, carry private information or attachments that were never meant to be shared, promise things the business cannot deliver, or strike a tone that does not match how Marrowbank Landscapes, Copperleaf Bakehouse or Tidewell Music School wish to be seen. Such slips can damage relationships, breach confidence and create awkward disputes. This procedure exists to keep outside communication accurate, appropriate and consistent, so that the business is represented well every time.

Start a run with procedures_start (procedure external-send@2, your task_id, action_class external_send), submit each enforced step's evidence with procedures_check, and pass the receipt you receive to email_send_external. The brain computes every check itself.

Steps
1. [enforced] c1 recipient-known: the To address is the email on file for the customer or contact. Evidence: {"to": ..., "contact_id": ...}.

- Send to an address that is not on file, even if a message came from it.

# Delete records (data-loss gate)
When to use: Use before deleting several records at once.

Background: Records hold the history of the business, including customer details, orders, lesson bookings, job notes and financial entries. Deleting several at once is risky because a single wrong selection can wipe out far more than intended, and removed information is often difficult or impossible to restore. Without a deliberate pause, people acting in a hurry may delete the wrong group of records, remove items still needed for legal, tax or customer-service reasons, or discover too late that something important has vanished. The damage can spread across Marrowbank Landscapes, Copperleaf Bakehouse and Tidewell Music School if shared information is affected. This procedure exists to make sure bulk deletion is intentional, understood and justified, protecting the business from avoidable and costly loss.

How to run it: This action is gated in the brain. Start a run with procedures_start (procedure data-loss-gate@1, your task_id, action_class deletion), submit each enforced step's evidence with procedures_check, and pass the receipt you receive to records_bulk_delete. The brain computes every check itself.

Steps
1. [enforced] c1 items-in-space: every record belongs to the business the request is about. Evidence: {"record_ids": [...]}.
2. [enforced] c2 no-retention-hold: no record is under a retention period or legal hold. Evidence: {"record_ids": [...]}.
3. [enforced, one-way: needs the owner] c3 owner-approval: the owner explicitly approves the deletion of these records. Evidence: {"tap_event_id": ...} from request_owner_approval.

Never:
- Delete a record under retention or legal hold.

Notes:
- Tax and contract records are kept 5 years; records in a dispute are on legal hold.
